title: Humidity Management and Transpiration Control
objective: Manage humidity as a water-loss control while preventing condensation, stagnation, and delayed acclimation.

terms.definition: The ratio of actual vapor pressure to saturation vapor pressure at the same air temperature, expressed as a percent.
Vapor pressure deficit: the difference between saturation vapor pressure and actual vapor pressure.
Loss of water vapor from plant tissues, primarily through stomata, as governed by vapor-pressure gradients and conductance.
The presence of liquid water on leaf or flower surfaces, whether from condensation, irrigation, or guttation.
Conversion of water vapor to liquid water on a surface at or below the local dew point.
Physiological regulation of stomatal aperture that changes gas exchange and water loss.
A local enclosure used in propagation to reduce vapor exchange and raise humidity around cuttings.

coreScience: Before roots form, cuttings have limited capacity to replace water lost from leaves. High surrounding humidity reduces the vapor-pressure gradient and can help maintain turgor during the most vulnerable period.

Humidity is not the only control. Leaf temperature, airflow, radiation, leaf area, tissue water status, and stomatal behavior influence loss. Condensation and persistent leaf wetness can favor some greenhouse foliar pathogens and can spread inoculum by splashing; disease response is pathogen-specific rather than universal.
Humidity should change with root development. A gradual transition toward the production environment tests whether roots and stomata can support the cutting without abrupt wilt.
cultivationRelevance: Measure the propagation-zone air near leaves, not only the room wall. Remove standing water, verify dome and tray cleanliness, and reduce humidity in controlled steps tied to rooting and recovery observations.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Air and leaf temperature; RH and VPD method; dome state; condensation and wetness duration; airflow; rooting stage; wilt and recovery after venting.

For humidity management and transpiration control, record the relevant developmental stage, environment, operator or treatment condition, and time sequence so the biological response can be separated from handling and facility effects.

Record the defined success endpoint, failures and off-types, replicate or batch variation, and any identity, health, rooting, survival, or follow-up test used to verify that the apparent result persisted after establishment.

misconceptions: Unrooted cuttings require 100% RH at all times. Visible similarity alone does not prove equivalent physiological state, health status, or later performance; identity and outcome measurements answer different questions.

A closed dome is automatically safe. A single observation or negative symptom check cannot exclude latent infection, developmental history, or protocol-specific effects; use the appropriate follow-up test or repeated observation.

Leaves standing upright proves the cutting has roots. Cultivar names, appearance, and one successful batch are not substitutes for traceable identity, controlled comparison, and repeatable propagation outcomes.
evidenceLimits: No single RH or VPD target applies to every cutting stage, cultivar, dome, light level, and airflow pattern.
